claim: EGFP-CHIP-transfected murine embryonic fibroblasts exposed to 43°C show cells with membranous CHIP localization.
source: Shortly upon exposing EGFP-CHIP-transfected murine embryonic fibroblasts to 43°C, cells with membranous CHIP localization could be identified (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a

claim: CHIP association with membranes is lost if samples are fixed with paraformaldehyde before microscopy.
source: CHIP association with membranes was lost if the samples had been fixed with paraformaldehyde before microscopy indicating a dynamic nature of the interaction.
evidence: Experimental observation indicating dynamic nature of interaction

claim: EGFP localization does not change during heat shock.
source: EGFP localization did not change during heat shock (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b

claim: Acute inhibition of HSP70 and HSP90 at 37°C leads to appearance of EGFP-CHIP at the plasma membrane.
source: At 37°C, acute inhibition of HSP70 and HSP90 with VER-155008 and 17-AAG, respectively, leads to the appearance of EGFP-CHIP, but not of EGFP, at the plasma membrane (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c) - similar to that taking place during heat shock.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c using specific inhibitors

claim: CHIP relocalization to membranes is not induced by arsenite treatment.
source: CHIP relocalization to membranes showed some specificity and was not induced by arsenite treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d

claim: CHIP loses its association with HSC70 during acute heat shock at 43°C for 60 min.
source: Indeed, transiently transfected CHIP partially lost its association with HSC70 during acute heat shock as determined by immunoprecipitation (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1b

claim: A fraction of endogenous CHIP in membranes exists in chaperone-free dimeric state.
source: Presence of a crosslinked dimer, even in the absence of the chaperone-competing peptide, in the membrane fraction (Figure 1c, lane 10) indicated that endogenous membrane-associated CHIP was at least partially chaperone-free.
evidence: Supported by subcellular fractionation and chemical crosslinking data in Figure 1c

claim: K30A mutant CHIP shows increased membrane localization compared to wild-type CHIP.
source: As predicted, a membranous localization of EGFP-CHIP-K30A was observed when compared to its wild-type version (Figure 1d).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data in Figure 1d

claim: Chaperone-free CHIP and K30A variant show similar binding patterns to phospholipids.
source: Chaperone-free CHIP and the K30A variant showed a similar binding pattern thus excluding accidental formation of a novel determinant of membrane association by the mutation. (Figure 1e).
evidence: Supported by lipid array data in Figure 1e

claim: CHIP shows specificity mainly to phosphatidic acid (PA) and phosphatidylinositol monophosphates (PIP), especially PI4P.
source: Finally, analysis of a broad spectrum of cellular phospholipids revealed CHIP specificity mainly to phosphatidic acid (PA) and phosphatidylinositol monophosphates (PIP), especially PI4P (Figure 1f).
evidence: Supported by lipid-binding assay data in Figure 1f

claim: CHIP binding to phosphatidylinositol-bisphosphates is reduced compared to monophosphates.
source: Binding to phosphatidylinositol-bisphosphates was reduced and there was no binding to phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-trisphosphate detected, arguing against a trivial electrostatic interaction but pointing instead to high stereospecificity (Sudhahar et al., 2008).
evidence: Experimental observation with citation to support stereospecificity interpretation

claim: CHIP does not bind to phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-trisphosphate.
source: Binding to phosphatidylinositol-bisphosphates was reduced and there was no binding to phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-trisphosphate detected, arguing against a trivial electrostatic interaction but pointing instead to high stereospecificity (Sudhahar et al., 2008).
evidence: Experimental observation with citation to support stereospecificity interpretation

claim: 20% PA enhances CHIP cofloatation with DOPC liposomes in floatation assays.
source: A liposome floatation assay revealed cofloatation of CHIP which was strongly enhanced when liposomes were supplemented with 20% PA (Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by liposome floatation assay data in Figure 2a

claim: PA and PI4P enhance CHIP association with liposomes in pelleting assays.
source: CHIP also interacted with liposomes in a liposome pelleting assay, in which pelleting was increased in the presence of PA and also by 1% PI4P, but to a lesser extent (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by liposome pelleting assay data in Figure 2b

claim: 5% PI4P strongly enhances association of liposomes with CHIP.
source: Increase of PI4P to 5% strongly enhanced association of liposomes with CHIP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by pelleting assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a

claim: 5% PA is insufficient to strengthen binding of CHIP onto liposomes.
source: On the other hand, 5% PA was insufficient to strengthen binding of CHIP onto liposomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by pelleting assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a

claim: CHIP associates with 20% PA- or 5% PI4P-containing liposomes very efficiently, reaching up to 50–60% of input values.
source: Notably, CHIP associated with 20% PA- or 5% PI4P-containing liposomes very efficiently, reaching up to 50–60% of input values, which allowed us to use Coomassie Blue-stained SDS-PAGE gels as readout.
evidence: Quantitative measurement from pelleting assays

claim: The TPR domain mediates binding of CHIP to liposomes.
source: The liposome cosedimentation analyses confirmed that the TPR domain is required for the interaction with membranes containing either PA or PI4P (Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by pelleting assay data with truncated proteins in Figure 2c

claim: The isolated TPR domain binds to PA-containing liposomes more strongly than the full-length protein.
source: Notably, the isolated TPR domain bound to the PA-containing liposomes more strongly than the parental full-length protein reaching ca. 160% efficiency of the full-length protein.
evidence: Quantitative comparison from pelleting assays

claim: Substoichiometric amounts (1 μM) of HSP70-C efficiently prevent CHIP from interacting with liposomes.
source: Surprisingly, even the substoichiometric amount of 1 μM HSP70-C efficiently prevented CHIP from interacting with liposomes (Figure 2d).
evidence: Supported by competition assay data in Figure 2d

claim: Preincubation of CHIP with equimolar amount of HSP70-C blocks association of CHIP with liposomes to ca. 30% of control.
source: Preincubation of CHIP with an equimolar amount of HSP70-C blocked the association of CHIP with liposomes to ca. 30% of the control.
evidence: Quantitative measurement from competition assays

claim: Ten-fold molar excess of HSP70-C results in complete loss of CHIP binding to phosphatidylinositol monophosphates and only residual interaction with phosphatidic acid.
source: Likewise, incubation of CHIP with lipid arrays in the presence of HSP70-C resulted in complete loss of binding to phosphatidylinositol monophosphates and only residual interaction with phosphatidic acid (Figure 2e).
evidence: Supported by lipid-binding assay data in Figure 2e

claim: TPR domain-less CHIP shows residual binding to phosphatidic acid-containing liposomes.
source: Because TPR domain-less CHIP still showed residual binding to phosphatidic acid-containing liposomes, we assumed additional lipid-interacting determinants.
evidence: Experimental observation leading to hypothesis of additional binding determinants

claim: CHIP contains two patches of positively charged amino acids: m1 (143–146 aa: KKKR) and m2 (221–225 aa: KRKKR).
source: Inspection of the CHIP sequence revealed two patches of positively charged amino acids which we named m1 (143–146 aa: KKKR) and m2 (221–225 aa: KRKKR) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Sequence analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a

claim: Both m1 and m2 motifs are outside of the TPR domain and are evolutionary conserved.
source: Both motifs are outside of the TPR domain and are evolutionary conserved (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment and structural analysis in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a

claim: m1 mutation to alanines does not affect specificity of lipid binding or association with cellular membranes.
source: When m1 was mutated to alanines, the specificity of lipid binding and association with cellular membranes was not affected (Figure 3b,c, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by lipid-binding assay and microscopy data in Figure 3b,c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b

claim: Partial exchange of m2 with alanines impairs CHIP-lipid interaction in vitro.
source: However, partial exchange of m2 with alanines impaired CHIP-lipid interaction in vitro (Figure 3b)
evidence: Supported by lipid-binding assay data in Figure 3b

claim: m2 mutation efficiently releases chaperone-free EGFP-CHIP-K30A from membranes in living cells.
source: However, partial exchange of m2 with alanines impaired CHIP-lipid interaction in vitro (Figure 3b) and efficiently released chaperone-free EGFP-CHIP-K30A from membranes in living cells (Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data in Figure 3c

claim: m2 mutant CHIP is present in both cytosol and nucleus, unlike wild-type CHIP.
source: Contrary to wild-type CHIP, m2 mutant was strongly present not only in the cytosol, but in the nucleus as well.
evidence: Observation from microscopy experiments

claim: CHIP remains dimeric on liposomes and is capable of oligomerization.
source: First, CHIP remained dimeric and was still capable of oligomerization (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by chemical crosslinking data in Figure 4a

claim: Monomerization of CHIP by deoxycholate reversibly inactivates its ubiquitin ligase activity.
source: This is an important finding since monomerization of CHIP by the steroid detergent deoxycholate (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a) was shown to reversibly inactivate its ubiquitin ligase activity (Nikolay et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by crosslinking data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a and citation to previous work

claim: The amount of secondary structure elements in CHIP does not change upon binding to liposomes.
source: The amount of secondary structure elements did not change upon binding to liposomes (Figure 4b)
evidence: Supported by CD spectroscopy data in Figure 4b

claim: The susceptibility of CHIP to protease hydrolysis on liposomes does not change.
source: Consistently, the susceptibility to protease hydrolysis on liposomes did not change (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by protease sensitivity assay data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b

claim: CHIP on liposomes can ubiquitylate substrate protein NQO1.
source: While attached to liposomes, CHIP remains capable to ubiquitylate the substrate protein NQO1 and form unattached K63-conjugated chains.
evidence: Supported by in vitro ubiquitylation assay data in Figure 4c

claim: CHIP on liposomes can form unattached K63-conjugated ubiquitin chains.
source: While attached to liposomes, CHIP remains capable to ubiquitylate the substrate protein NQO1 and form unattached K63-conjugated chains.
evidence: Supported by in vitro ubiquitylation assay data in Figure 4c

claim: Auto-ubiquitylation of CHIP proceeds somewhat stronger on liposomes.
source: Auto-ubiquitylation of CHIP is supported by UbcH5a as well (Zhang et al., 2005) and seemed to proceed somewhat stronger on liposomes (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by in vitro ubiquitylation assay data in Figure 4c and citation

claim: K63-based ubiquitin polymerization by CHIP is slightly weaker on liposomes.
source: K63-based ubiquitin polymerization by CHIP does not require a substrate protein (Zhang et al., 2005) and, contrary to auto-ubiquitylation, was slightly weaker on liposomes (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by in vitro ubiquitylation assay data in Figure 4c and citation

claim: Ubiquitin K63-linking activity regulates membrane-related processes such as receptor internalization, multivesicular body formation and autophagy.
source: Ubiquitin K63-linking activity is especially interesting because it is known to regulate a number of membrane-related processes, such as receptor internalization, multivesicular body formation and autophagy (Erpapazoglou et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: Early translocation of HSF1 into nucleus during heat shock is not affected by the absence of CHIP.
source: CHIP was implicated in HSF1 activation during stress response (Dai et al., 2003). However, early translocation of HSF1 into nucleus during heat shock was not affected by the absence of CHIP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by nuclei isolation data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b and citation

claim: PLD isoform-unspecific inhibitor FIPI and PLD1 inhibitor VU0155069 efficiently release chaperone-free CHIP into the cytosol.
source: The PLD isoform-unspecific inhibitor FIPI and the inhibitor of PLD1 (VU0155069), but not that of PLD2 (CAY10594), efficiently released chaperone-free CHIP into the cytosol (Figure 5a).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data in Figure 5a

claim: PLD2 inhibitor CAY10594 does not release chaperone-free CHIP into the cytosol.
source: The PLD isoform-unspecific inhibitor FIPI and the inhibitor of PLD1 (VU0155069), but not that of PLD2 (CAY10594), efficiently released chaperone-free CHIP into the cytosol (Figure 5a).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data in Figure 5a

claim: PLD inhibitors do not change the abundance of CHIP.
source: This was not due to changes in the abundance of CHIP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c)
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1c

claim: PLD inhibitors do not cause general disturbance of membrane structure.
source: This was not due to changes in the abundance of CHIP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c) or general disturbance of membrane structure as controlled by the correct localization of farnesylated EGFP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data of farnesylated EGFP in Figure 5—figure supplement 1d

claim: Inhibitors of PI4P-generating type III phosphoinositol-4 kinases (PI4KIII) release chaperone-free CHIP from the plasma membrane.
source: From the other side, it was also possible to release chaperone-free CHIP from the plasma membrane using inhibitors of PI4P-generating type III phosphoinositol-4 kinases (PI4KIII) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1e,f).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1e,f

claim: Wortmannin inhibits PI4KIII at higher concentrations despite being a specific inhibitor of PI3K.
source: Wortmannin is a specific inhibitor of PI3K, however, it inhibits PI4KIII if used at higher concentrations (Nakanishi et al., 1995).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: More proteins interact with chaperone-free CHIP when it is released into the cytosol compared to membrane-bound state.
source: Interestingly, more proteins interacted with chaperone-free CHIP when it was released into the cytosol (Figure 5b) suggesting pronounced 'stickiness' of the mislocalized ligase.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 5b

claim: The overlap between CHIP substrate sets in control and PLD1 inhibition conditions is minimal.
source: The overlap between substrate sets was minimal (Figure 5c), which can be considered as biochemical verification of altered localization upon PLD1 inhibition.
evidence: Supported by Venn diagram in Figure 5c

claim: Most CHIP interactors reside at the plasma membrane or at one of the organelles.
source: Most of the interactors reside at the plasma membrane or at one of the organelles confirming the broad potential of chaperone-free CHIP to modify cellular architecture (Figure 5d).
evidence: Supported by subcellular localization analysis in Figure 5d

claim: 56 proteins show significant abundance changes upon CHIP overexpression.
source: Correlation of the measured intensities from four independent experiments revealed robust repeatability resulting in a highly overlapping set of measured proteins (Figure 5—figure supplement 1h) and allowing identification of 56 significant changes (Figure 5e, Figure 5—source data 4).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 5e

claim: More proteins show reduced abundance (37) than increased abundance (19) upon CHIP overexpression.
source: There were more proteins with a reduced rather than an increased abundance, 37 versus 19, respectively, which is an expected bias considering the involvement of CHIP in protein degradation.
evidence: Quantitative analysis from mass spectrometry with interpretation based on CHIP's known function

claim: 'Golgi organization' GOBPslim term is the second-highest enrichment among significantly changed proteins upon CHIP overexpression.
source: GO analysis of CHIP interactors scored 'Golgi organization' GOBPslim term (biological processes) as the second-highest enrichment among significantly changed proteins (Figure 5f).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis in Figure 5f

claim: The Golgi apparatus fragments under heat shock.
source: This is especially interesting because the Golgi apparatus is known to fragment under heat shock (Petrosyan and Cheng, 2014; Welch and Suhan, 1985).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: CHIP overexpression causes fragmentation of the Golgi apparatus.
source: Coexpression of the β−1,4-galactosyltransferase1-EGFP marker (Cole et al., 1996) verified fragmentation of the Golgi apparatus following CHIP overexpression (Figure 5g).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data in Figure 5g and citation

claim: CHIP-deficient fibroblasts fail to increase fragmentation of the Golgi apparatus during heat shock.
source: In a complementary setup, CHIP-deficient fibroblasts failed to increase fragmentation of the Golgi apparatus during heat shock (Figure 5h) further supporting the involvement of CHIP in the reorganization of membrane-bound organelles during proteostasis stress.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data in Figure 5h

claim: Overexpression of HSP70 inhibits fragmentation of the Golgi apparatus by CHIP.
source: The central role of chaperone availability in this mechanism is supported by the observation that the overexpression of HSP70 inhibited fragmentation of the Golgi apparatus by CHIP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1j).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1j

claim: Golgi integral membrane protein 4 (Golim4) is reduced to 62% of normal levels upon CHIP overexpression.
source: Some proteins showed lower abundance, for example, Golgi integral membrane protein 4 (Golim4) was reduced to 62% of its normal levels
evidence: Quantitative measurement from mass spectrometry

claim: The amount of Rab GDP dissociation inhibitor Gdi2 doubles upon CHIP overexpression.
source: others were upregulated, for example, the amount of Rab GDP dissociation inhibitor Gdi2 doubled.
evidence: Quantitative measurement from mass spectrometry

claim: CHIP was initially identified as a cytosolic cochaperone.
source: Initially identified as a cytosolic cochaperone (Ballinger et al., 1999), CHIP was shortly afterwards discovered to be a U-box E3 ubiquitin ligase.
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: CHIP is a U-box E3 ubiquitin ligase.
source: Initially identified as a cytosolic cochaperone (Ballinger et al., 1999), CHIP was shortly afterwards discovered to be a U-box E3 ubiquitin ligase.
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: CHIP engages with HSP70 and HSP90 molecular chaperones which act as adaptors to detect substrate proteins.
source: It was found to engage with HSP70 and HSP90 molecular chaperones which act as adaptors to detect substrate proteins (Jiang et al., 2001; Murata et al., 2001).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: CHIP interacts with chaperones through the N-terminal tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) domain.
source: CHIP interacts with the chaperones through the N-terminal tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) domain.
evidence: Established knowledge about CHIP structure-function

claim: The C-terminal tails of chaperones determine the specificity and affinity of association with CHIP.
source: The C-terminal tails of chaperones determines the specificity and affinity of this association, which is rather low (Wang et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: The association between CHIP and chaperones is rather low affinity.
source: The C-terminal tails of chaperones determines the specificity and affinity of this association, which is rather low (Wang et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: Weak interaction between CHIP and chaperones implies dynamic and transient collaboration.
source: Weak interaction implies dynamic and transient collaboration between CHIP and the chaperones; however, a detailed atomic and kinetic understanding of the collaboration is missing.
evidence: Inference from known weak interaction

claim: Cells accumulate damaged proteins in distinct subcellular structures and inherit them asymmetrically in mother and daughter cells.
source: At the level of single cells, an obvious strategy to deal with proteostasis load is to accumulate it in distinct subcellular structures and, in the case of duplication, to inherit it asymmetrically in mother and daughter cells (Escusa-Toret et al., 2013; Kaganovich et al., 2008; Miller et al., 2015; Sontag et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: Several cellular locations are used to concentrate damaged proteins, such as the perinuclear endoplasmic reticulum or perivacuolar space.
source: Several cellular locations are used to concentrate damaged proteins, such as the perinuclear endoplasmic reticulum or perivacuolar space (Kaganovich et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: HSP70, HSP90, HSP40, and HSP110 are involved in sorting misfolded proteins to deposition sites.
source: A number of PN components, including molecular chaperones from HSP70 and HSP90 families but also the cochaperones HSP40 and HSP110, were shown to be involved in sorting misfolded proteins to the deposition sites (Sontag et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: The ΔF508 mutant of chloride channel CFTR is a well-known substrate of CHIP.
source: The best-known example among its substrates is the ΔF508 mutant of chloride channel CFTR (Meacham et al., 2001).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: CHIP participates in quality control of plasma membrane-resident proteins.
source: In addition to the endoplasmic reticulum-related quality control, CHIP has been shown to participate in the quality control of plasma membrane-resident proteins (Okiyoneda et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: Quality control of plasma membrane-resident proteins by CHIP entails participation of HSP70 and HSP90.
source: This activity also entails the participation of HSP70 and HSP90 (Okiyoneda et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: In plants, PA is involved in response to many diverse stressors including high salt, drought, cold, and aluminium exposure.
source: First, in plants PA is known to be involved in response to many diverse stressors, such as high salt, drought, cold, aluminium exposure, to mention a few (Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: The constitutive levels of PA in membranes are comparably high but can change to functionally significant extents depending on metabolic or stress conditions.
source: Second, the constitutive levels of PA in membranes are comparably high, yet they can change to functionally significant extents depending on metabolic or stress conditions (Fang et al., 2001).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: Phospholipase D family enzymes have been associated with diverse pathologies including Alzheimer's disease.
source: Third, the involvement of PA-generating enzymes from the phospholipase D family in diverse pathologies has been established, advancing the development of therapeutics and thus creating possibilities to intervene (Frohman, 2015). In this regard, Alzheimer's disease is an interesting example, having been associated with different isoforms of phospholipase D.
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: PI3P is enriched on early endosomes.
source: For example, PI3P is enriched on early endosomes and PI4P marks the Golgi apparatus and plasma membrane (Hammond and Balla, 2015).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: PI4P marks the Golgi apparatus and plasma membrane.
source: For example, PI3P is enriched on early endosomes and PI4P marks the Golgi apparatus and plasma membrane (Hammond and Balla, 2015).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: PI3P and PI5P are less abundant than PI4P (ca. ten and hundred times, respectively).
source: PI3P and PI5P are less abundant than PI4P (ca. ten and hundred times, respectively) (Hammond and Balla, 2015)
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: HSF1-driven activation of stress gene transcription is a transcriptional reaction to cytosolic stress.
source: Immediate reorganization and adaptation of organelles is a less understood aspect of cytosolic stress response compared to the transcriptional and post-transcriptional reactions, such as HSF1-driven activation of stress gene transcription (Akerfelt et al., 2010)
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: eIF2α-mediated attenuation of protein synthesis is a post-transcriptional reaction to cytosolic stress.
source: Immediate reorganization and adaptation of organelles is a less understood aspect of cytosolic stress response compared to the transcriptional and post-transcriptional reactions, such as HSF1-driven activation of stress gene transcription (Akerfelt et al., 2010) or eIF2α-mediated attenuation of protein synthesis (Schneider and Bertolotti, 2015).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: Golgi fragmentation is a marker or cause of cellular toxicity upon different stressors, including protein aggregation.
source: Although reversible under limited heat shock, Golgi fragmentation is a well-known marker or even the cause of cellular toxicity upon different stressors, including protein aggregation (Alvarez-Miranda et al., 2015; Haase and Rabouille, 2015).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: Dissociation of CHIP from molecular chaperones under conformational stress resembles activation of HSF1.
source: Dissociation of CHIP from molecular chaperones under conformational stress resembles activation of HSF1 when the liberated protein trimerizes and translocates to the site of its transcriptional activity (Morimoto, 1993).
evidence: Comparison to known mechanism with citation

claim: Liberated HSF1 trimerizes and translocates to the site of its transcriptional activity.
source: Dissociation of CHIP from molecular chaperones under conformational stress resembles activation of HSF1 when the liberated protein trimerizes and translocates to the site of its transcriptional activity (Morimoto, 1993).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: HOP, DnaJC7, FKBP51, and FKBP52 engage their TPR domains to interact with HSP70 and HSP90.
source: In addition to CHIP, a number of other members from the PN, such as HOP, DnaJC7, FKBP51, FKBP52 among others, engage their TPR domains to interact with HSP70 and HSP90 (Assimon et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: C-terminal phosphorylation of HSP70 and HSP90 critically affects TPR domain-based associations.
source: For example, C-terminal phosphorylation of HSP70 and HSP90, such as that which takes place during a proliferative boost, was shown to critically affect TPR domain-based associations (Muller et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: The mammalian ubiquitin ligase CHIP can dock on cellular membranes when freed from chaperones during acute stress.
source: Here we show that the mammalian ubiquitin ligase C-terminal Hsp70-interacting protein (CHIP), if freed from chaperones during acute stress, can dock on cellular membranes thus performing a proteostasis sensor function.
evidence: Main finding of the study summarized in abstract

claim: HSP70 and membranes compete for mutually exclusive binding to the tetratricopeptide repeat domain of CHIP.
source: HSP70 and membranes compete for mutually exclusive binding to the tetratricopeptide repeat domain of CHIP.
evidence: Main finding of the study summarized in abstract

claim: CHIP participates in the fragmentation of the Golgi apparatus as an effector function.
source: At new cellular locations, access to compartment-specific substrates would enable CHIP to participate in the reorganization of the respective organelles, as exemplified by the fragmentation of the Golgi apparatus (effector function).
evidence: Main finding of the study summarized in abstract

claim: The proteostasis network is responsible for protein refolding and degradation in case of unrepairable damage.
source: To keep the cellular proteome in structural and functional balance, called proteostasis, a network of specialized proteins has evolved (Balch et al., 2008; Balchin et al., 2016). The proteostasis network (PN) is responsible for protein refolding and, in case of the unrepairable damage, degradation.
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: Different classes of molecular chaperones assist during refolding and E3 ubiquitin ligases are involved in degradation function.
source: Different classes of molecular chaperones assist during refolding and E3 ubiquitin ligases are involved in degradation function (Amm et al., 2014; Balchin et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: CHIP is a paradigm example of how protein folding and degradation pathways cooperate during protein quality control.
source: C-terminal Hsp70-interacting protein (CHIP) is a paradigm example of how protein folding and degradation pathways cooperate during protein quality control (Arndt et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: Considerable progress has been achieved in elucidating signaling and metabolic mechanisms associated with proteostasis changes during organism aging.
source: Considerable progress has been achieved in elucidating signaling and metabolic mechanisms associated with proteostasis changes during organism aging (Ben-Zvi et al., 2009; Taylor and Dillin, 2011)
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: There are differences in PN composition and stress response across tissues.
source: Considerable progress has been achieved in elucidating signaling and metabolic mechanisms associated with proteostasis changes during organism aging (Ben-Zvi et al., 2009; Taylor and Dillin, 2011) and differences of PN composition and stress response across tissues (Guisbert et al., 2013; Tebbenkamp and Borchelt, 2010).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: Protein phosphatase 5 binds fatty acids through its TPR domain.
source: However, there is at least one example of a TPR domain-lipid interaction as in the case of protein phosphatase 5 binding fatty acids (Chen and Cohen, 1997).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: The N-terminal tail of CHIP is very dynamic extending flexibility over the first two α-helices in the TPR domain.
source: According to deuterium exchange measurements, the N-terminal tail is very dynamic extending this flexibility over the first two α-helices in the TPR domain (Graf et al., 2010)
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: 16 C-terminal α-helical amino acids cap the last tetratricopeptide repeat of CHIP.
source: from the other side, 16 C-terminal α-helical amino acids seem to cap the last tetratricopeptide repeat (Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: The K30A mutation in CHIP affects binding to HSP70 as measured by isothermal titration calorimetry.
source: Isothermal titration calorimetry using octapeptide GPTIEEVD confirmed the weak binding to wild-type CHIP (Kd = 5 μM when measured at 37°C) which was further reduced in case of K30A mutant (Figure 1—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: Supported by ITC data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1h

claim: Wild-type CHIP binds to HSP70 octapeptide GPTIEEVD with Kd = 5 μM at 37°C.
source: Isothermal titration calorimetry using octapeptide GPTIEEVD confirmed the weak binding to wild-type CHIP (Kd = 5 μM when measured at 37°C)
evidence: Quantitative measurement from ITC

claim: CHIP naturally exists as a dimer.
source: In preliminary experiments with recombinant protein, the conditions to capture CHIP in its naturally dimeric state (Nikolay et al., 2004) were established
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: Basic amino acid motifs in polypeptides often play an important role in recognition of negatively charged phospholipids.
source: Basic amino acid motifs in polypeptides often play an important role in recognition of negatively charged phospholipids (Stahelin et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: CHIP can collaborate with several E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes providing similar binding surface for interaction.
source: As an E3 ubiquitin ligase, CHIP collaborates with several E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes providing similar binding surface for interaction (Xu et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: NQO1 P187S mutant is ubiquitylated by CHIP with and without assistance of chaperones.
source: NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1) P187S mutant served as a substrate protein because it is known to be ubiquitylated by CHIP with and without assistance of chaperones (Martínez-Limón et al., 2016; Tsvetkov et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: K63-based ubiquitin polymerization by CHIP does not require a substrate protein.
source: K63-based ubiquitin polymerization by CHIP does not require a substrate protein (Zhang et al., 2005)
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: Hydrolysis of phosphatidylcholine by phospholipase D family generates phosphatidic acid (PA).
source: One of the cellular pathways that generates CHIP-interacting phosphatidic acid (PA) is the hydrolysis of phosphatidylcholine by members of the phospholipase D (PLD) family (Foster et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from previous work

claim: The K30A mutation in CHIP does not affect interaction with E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes according to one report.
